newsitem.title: FRANCE: Domestic pressures strain Franco-German euro drive.
newsitem.headline: Domestic pressures strain Franco-German euro drive.

text.p: The conventional wisdom in European politics is that when the Franco-German locomotive breaks down, the European train stops in its tracks.

That overworked cliche has rarely been more true than today, when conflicting domestic pressures in France and Germany are shaking the ambitious drive to launch a single European currency by the end of the decade.

The election of a left-wing French government pledged to public job-creation programmes and against austerity, coinciding with deepening financial problems and political challenges facing jaded German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, has strained the Paris-Bonn partnership more seriously than for decades.
They disagree about austerity, they differ on defence and NATO and they were at odds about jobs policy and the future of European Union institutions at last month's Amsterdam EU summit.

Yet they still agree on the overriding aim of launching the single currency on time in January 1999 and European diplomats are convinced that will force Kohl and Socialist French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin to overcome their current problems.

Diplomats said the two leaders, whose first meeting last month was distinctly cool, were likely to meet informally this summer, if only to signal their joint determination to go ahead with economic and monetary union.
But one diplomat closely involved in Franco-German ties said: "Both men are too absorbed in their domestic problems to have a real clarification."

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has said France's public deficit this year will be "significantly higher" than the three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) set as a target in the Maastricht treaty to qualify for monetary union.
Strauss-Kahn brushed off journalists who pressed him on Thursday about Kohl's insistence this week that Germany considered the target meant "3.0 percent".
"It won't have escaped your notice that Mr Kohl speaks for Germany and the French government speaks for France," he said.
Repeating that Paris too wanted to respect "the treaty, the whole treaty and nothing but the treaty", he added: "It is clear that some people can have different readings of the treaty."
Strauss-Kahn has said France will definitely miss 3.0 percent but will take steps to curb this year's deficit and wants the Maastricht criteria interpreted as a trend.

Kohl's top deputy, Wolfgang Schaeuble, said on Wednesday the launch of the euro could run into trouble if France's deficit were to reach about 3.6 percent of GDP, as an audit of public finances is expected to show.
"It would be a problem if it came to a budget deficit of this size in France," Schaeuble said, adding he hoped the new government would make serious efforts to limit this year's deficit.

Diplomats said the two governments faced conflicting pressures from their electorates. Kohl was under strong pressure from the right-wing Bavarian Christian Social Union in his coalition to stick to fiscal orthodoxy, given German voters' attachment to a strong deutschemark and allergy to inflation.

Jospin, by contrast, was elected because French voters were fed up with austerity and high unemployment blamed on the drive to cut public deficits. He is under pressure in his rainbow left-wing coalition to reflate a sluggish economy and avoid further sacrifices.

The diplomats said Bonn could probably live with a French deficit of 3.3 to 3.4 percent, especially since its own deficit could be around 3.2 percent despite new measures Kohl is due to announce on July 11.
Another Kohl associate, Christian Democratic European expert Karl Lamers, told Reuters it was important that the new French government be seen to be taking action to reduce its deficit.

Lamers said there was an urgent need for Paris and Bonn to clear the air and get to the bottom of their differences, after the failure of last month's Poitiers Franco-German summit and tension at the Amsterdam European Union summit.
He voiced confidence that Jospin would quickly recognise there was no alternative policy.
The French daily Le Figaro summed up the state of ties with the headline: "Paris-Bonn, raw nerves."
